source_lines.43: Take two independent Bernoulli samples of sizes $n_1,n_2\ge1$ and test the one-sided alternative that the first success probability exceeds the second. Under the null, all $N=n_1+n_2$ trials have a common success probability $p\in[0,1]$. Let $K$ be the number of successes in the first sample and $S$ the total number in both samples. For every integer margin $s\in\{0,\ldots,N\}$, define the supplied conditional-law kernel $Q$ by
source_lines.45: and set $Q(s,\{k\})=0$ outside the displayed range. For each $s$, these weights sum to one because they count all $\binom Ns$ ways to choose the $s$ success positions according to how many lie in the first sample. At margins of positive probability this is the conditional law and it does not depend on $p$; at endpoint nulls $p=0,1$, the formula also supplies a version at the other, probability-zero margins. Large values of $K$ support the one-sided alternative that the first sample has a larger success probability. For $n_1=n_2=2$ and $s=2$, the conditional masses at $k=0,1,2$ are $1/6,4/6,1/6$; the inclusive upper-tail p-values are $1,5/6,1/6$.
source_lines.67: 2.1 There are $\binom{N}{s}$ sequences with $s$ successes. Exactly $\binom{n_1}{k}\binom{n_2}{s-k}$ of them have $K=k$: choose $k$ of the first $n_1$ positions and $s-k$ of the other $n_2$. These counts partition all size-$s$ subsets, so the displayed kernel weights sum to one for every $s$, and when $P_p(S=s)>0$, dividing by the total count using [F3] gives the conditional mass; the feasible range is precisely where both binomial coefficients are nonzero. At $p=0$ only $S=0$ occurs and $K=0$; at $p=1$ only $S=N$ occurs and $K=n_1$, so the supplied kernel has the required conditional law on the realized margin. At the other, probability-zero margins the same formula is simply the chosen kernel extension. [F1, F3, step 1.1, given, construct, algebra]

source_lines.53: Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $X_i$ be iid $N(\mu,1)$, let the full parameter space be $\Theta=\mathbb R$, and test $H_0:\mu\le0$ against the full model at the boundary value $\mu=0$. The likelihood-ratio statistic converges to $(G\vee0)^2$, where $G\sim N(0,1)$; by [[def-chi-square-law]] this is $\tfrac12\chi_0^2+\tfrac12\chi_1^2$, not the ordinary $\chi_1^2$ law.
source_lines.103: 4.1 Under $\mu=0$, the local sets are $C_n=\mathbb R$ and $C_{0n}=(-\infty,0]$ for every $n$, so they are already their limiting closed convex cones. Direct expansion gives $\ell_n(h/\sqrt n)-\ell_n(0)=hZ_n-h^2/2$ with $Z_n=\sqrt n\bar X_n$ and zero remainder. The full and null local maximizers are $Z_n$ and $\min(0,Z_n)$. By [F4] and the mean and variance from step 1.1, $Z_n\Rightarrow G\sim N(0,1)$. Choose a large $R$ with $P(|G|\ge R)$ small and apply [F5] to the closed tails to see that both maximizer sequences are tight. Thus all hypotheses of [F3] hold with $I=1$. [A1, F3, F4, F5, given, step 1.1, choose, algebra, step 3.1]
source_lines.105: 5.1 Completing the square in $\ell_n(\mu)$ gives the full MLE $\bar X_n$ and the constrained MLE $\min(0,\bar X_n)$. Hence the finite-sample likelihood-ratio statistic is $T_n=2[\ell_n(\bar X_n)-\ell_n(\min(0,\bar X_n))]=n(\bar X_n\vee0)^2=(Z_n\vee0)^2$. By [F5], $T_n\Rightarrow(G\vee0)^2$. Its CDF is $0$ for $t<0$ and $P(G\le\sqrt t)=\Phi(\sqrt t)$ for $t\ge0$, so it has mass $1/2$ at zero. By symmetry, $P(G^2\le t)=2\Phi(\sqrt t)-1$ for $t\ge0$, while [F1] gives $P(G=0)=0$; hence $(G\vee0)^2$ has the mixture law $\tfrac12\delta_0+\tfrac12\mathcal L(G^2)=\tfrac12\chi_0^2+\tfrac12\chi_1^2$, not $\chi_1^2$. [A1, F1, F2, F5, step 4.1, given, algebra] ∎

source_lines.60: 1.1 For each coordinate $i$, define $\phi_i(x)=K(x,\{z\in\mathbb R^d:z_i\ge a/2\})$. This is a measurable $[0,1]$-valued function by [F2]. If the true bit is $0$, an action counted by $\phi_i$ has coordinate squared error at least $a^2/4$; if the true bit is $1$, an action outside that event has coordinate squared error at least $a^2/4$. Thus $R_\omega(K)\ge\frac{a^2}{4}\sum_{i=1}^d \bigl[(1-\omega_i)\,P_\omega\phi_i+\omega_i\,P_\omega(1-\phi_i)\bigr],$ where $P f:=\int f\,dP$. [F1, F2, F3, given, algebra]
source_lines.62: 2.1 For any two probability laws $P,Q$ and measurable $\phi:\mathcal X\to[0,1]$, the finite approximants $\phi_N=N^{-1}\sum_{r=1}^N\mathbf1_{\{\phi\ge r/N\}}$ satisfy $0\le\phi-\phi_N\le1/N$. By [F4], $\int\phi_NdP-\int\phi_NdQ\le\|P-Q\|_{\rm TV}$, and the replacement error is at most $2/N$. Letting $N\to\infty$ gives $\int\phi dP-\int\phi dQ\le\|P-Q\|_{\rm TV}$. Applying the same result to $1-\phi$ gives $P\phi+Q(1-\phi)\ge1-\|P-Q\|_{\rm TV}.$ For each coordinate, pair every hypercube vertex with bit $i=0$ to the unique neighbor with bit $i=1$. There are $2^{d-1}$ such pairs, and each pair's two testing errors in step 1.1 sum to at least $1-v$. Averaging over all $2^d$ vertices therefore gives average coordinate error at least $(1-v)/2$. This establishes the coordinate error bound. [F4, step 1.1, algebra]

source_lines.94: 1.1 By full column rank, the columns of $X$ are linearly independent. Apply [F2] to obtain orthonormal columns of $Q\in\mathbb R^{n\times p}$ with the same successive spans. Expressing each column of $X$ in this basis gives $X=QR$, where $R$ is upper triangular; its diagonal entries are the nonzero Gram–Schmidt residual norms, so $R$ is invertible. Let $W=\operatorname{col}X$. The columns of $X$ form a basis of $W$, so $\dim W=p$. By [F3], $\mathbb R^n=W\oplus W^\perp$. The subspace $W^\perp$ is finite-dimensional by [F10], and direct-sum dimension additivity in [F10] gives $n=p+\dim W^\perp$, hence $\dim W^\perp=n-p$. By [F3], choose an orthonormal basis of this complement with exactly $n-p$ vectors as the columns of $Q_0$; together with $Q$ it forms an orthonormal basis $[Q\ Q_0]$ of $\mathbb R^n$. [F2, F3, F10, choose, algebra]
source_lines.96: 2.1 Set $U=[Q\ Q_0]$. Then $U$ is orthogonal. Standardizing the independent errors gives $\eta=\varepsilon/\sigma$ with independent standard-normal coordinates, so [F4] makes $U^T\eta=(Z_Q,Z_0)$ a standard-normal product vector with independent coordinate blocks. Since $X=QR$ and $X^TX=R^TR$, the normal-equation solution in [F1] is $\widehat\beta=R^{-1}Q^TY=\beta+\sigma R^{-1}Z_Q$. Substituting $X=QR$ and $(R^TR)^{-1}=R^{-1}R^{-T}$ gives $P_X=Q R(R^TR)^{-1}R^TQ^T=Q[RR^{-1}R^{-T}R^T]Q^T=QQ^T$, because $RR^{-1}=I_p$ and $R^{-T}R^T=I_p$. Since $U$ is orthogonal, $I_n-P_X=Q_0Q_0^T$. Thus $(I_n-P_X)Y=\sigma Q_0Z_0$, so $RSS_X/\sigma^2=\|Z_0\|^2\sim\chi_{n-p}^2$ by [F5]. By [A2] and [F7], the linear maps defining $\widehat\beta$ and $Q_0Z_0$, and the squared-norm map defining $RSS_X$, are Borel; hence these quantities are measurable functions of the independent coordinate blocks and $\widehat\beta$ is independent of $RSS_X$ by [F4]. The map defining $\widehat\beta$ is linear and Borel, so it is a statistic for the stated experiment. The residual map and squared norm are continuous, so $RSS_X$ and $S$ are continuous. The piecewise t version in the Statement is Borel: its quotient is continuous on the Borel set $S>0$ and its value on $S=0$ is constant. Its denominator has positive degree $n-p$, hence $S>0$ almost surely by [F5]. [A1, A2, F1, F4, F5, F7, step 1.1, algebra]
source_lines.100: 4.1 For the nested models, let $W_D=W_U\cap W_R^\perp$. For $u\in W_U$, its orthogonal decomposition relative to $W_R$ has a $W_R$ component and a remaining component in $W_U\cap W_R^\perp=W_D$, because $W_R\subseteq W_U$. Thus [F3] gives $W_U=W_R\oplus W_D$ and $\mathbb R^n=W_U\oplus W_U^\perp$. All these subspaces are finite-dimensional by [F10]. Applying direct-sum dimension additivity in [F10] to the two decompositions gives $p=(p-q)+\dim W_D$ and $n=p+\dim W_U^\perp$, hence $\dim W_D=q$ and $\dim W_U^\perp=n-p$. Combining the orthogonal decompositions gives $\mathbb R^n=W_R\oplus W_D\oplus W_U^\perp$, including the zero-dimensional $W_R$ case $q=p$. Choose orthonormal bases in these three spaces and concatenate them into an orthogonal matrix $V$. By [F4], the coordinates of $V^T\varepsilon/\sigma$ in the three blocks are independent standard normals. Under the null, $P_R(X\beta)=P_U(X\beta)=X\beta$, so $(I-P_R)Y=(I-P_R)\varepsilon=P_{W_D}\varepsilon+P_{W_U^\perp}\varepsilon$ and $(I-P_U)Y=(I-P_U)\varepsilon=P_{W_U^\perp}\varepsilon$: here [F8] identifies $I-P_R=P_{W_R^\perp}$ and $I-P_U=P_{W_U^\perp}$, while the direct sum in [F3] splits the first projection into the two orthogonal components. The coordinate-block maps and the linear projections are continuous, and squared norms are continuous, so [A2] and [F7] make all these random vectors and real variables measurable. Orthogonality and [F9] give $RSS_R-RSS_U=\sigma^2\sum_{j=1}^{q}G_j^2$ and $RSS_U=\sigma^2\sum_{j=1}^{n-p}H_j^2$, where the $G$ and $H$ coordinate blocks are independent standard-normal blocks. By [F5] these sums are independent $\sigma^2\chi_q^2$ and $\sigma^2\chi_{n-p}^2$ variables; both degrees are positive. The piecewise ratio $\widetilde F$ is Borel, since it is continuous on the Borel set $RSS_U>0$ and constant on $RSS_U=0$. Its value is the scaled ratio on $Q_H:=\sum_{j=1}^{n-p}H_j^2>0$ and $0$ when $Q_H=0$; by [F6] this is exactly the defined $F_{q,n-p}$ version. The F denominator is positive almost surely by [F5], so $\widetilde F\sim F_{q,n-p}$. [A1, A2, F3, F4, F5, F6, F7, F8, F9, F10, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

source_lines.22: Let $p\in\mathbb N_0$ and let $\xi$ be a clamped knot vector as in [[def-b-spline-space-and-basis]]. The recursively defined degree-$p$ B-splines are nonnegative, are supported on $[\xi_j,\xi_{j+p+1}]$, and are piecewise polynomials of degree at most $p$. At a knot of multiplicity $\mu\le p$, each B-spline is $C^{p-\mu}$; multiplicity $p+1$ imposes no continuity requirement. On every nonempty knot interval $[\xi_m,\xi_{m+1})$, the active functions $B_{m-p,p,\xi},\ldots,B_{m,p,\xi}$ form a basis of $\mathcal P_p$ and sum to one. Globally, the $n$ B-splines form a basis of $S_{p,\xi}$. In particular, every $q\in\mathcal P_p$ has a unique expansion $q=\sum_{j=1}^n c_jB_{j,p,\xi}$ on $[a,b]$.
source_lines.36: 1.1 For $p=0$, support, piecewise degree, and nonnegativity follow from the indicator definition in [F1]. Inductively, each degree-$p$ term is a lower-degree spline multiplied by an affine factor; on the lower-degree spline's support that factor is nonnegative, and the two supports lie inside $[\xi_j, \xi_{j+p+1}]$. Thus support, degree at most $p$, and nonnegativity hold for every $p$. [A1, F1, algebra]
source_lines.40: 2.1 Define $\psi_{j,0}(y)=1$ and $\psi_{j,d}(y)=\prod_{r=1}^{d}(y-\xi_{j+r})$. When $\xi_{j+d}>\xi_j$, factoring $\psi_{j,d-1}$ gives $(y-x)\psi_{j,d-1}(y)=\frac{x-\xi_j}{\xi_{j+d}-\xi_j}\psi_{j,d}(y)+\frac{\xi_{j+d}-x}{\xi_{j+d}-\xi_j}\psi_{j-1,d}(y)$. Fix a nonempty cell $[\xi_m,\xi_{m+1})$. At degree zero its sole nonzero indicator is $B_{m,0,\xi}$, so the local identity holds. Inductively, the degree-$(d-1)$ local sum has indices $m-d+1\le j\le m$. For every such index, $\xi_j\le\xi_m<\xi_{m+1}\le\xi_{j+d}$, so the displayed identity has a strictly positive denominator. Multiply that local sum by $y-x$, apply the identity, and regroup with [F1]. The two extra lower-degree functions $B_{m-d,d-1,\xi}$ and $B_{m+1,d-1,\xi}$ vanish on the cell by support, even when their supports are empty; their recurrence terms are zero under [F1]. Thus $(y-x)^d=\sum_{i=m-d}^{m}\psi_{i,d}(y)B_{i,d,\xi}(x)$ for $0\le d\le p$, and in particular for $d=p$. [F1, given, step 1.1, algebra]
source_lines.44: 3.2 Fix an open nonempty knot interval $(\xi_m,\xi_{m+1})$ and $p\ge1$. The $p+1$ dual polynomials $\psi_{i,p}$, $m-p\le i\le m$, form a basis of $\mathcal P_p$ in $y$: differentiating the identity of step 2.1 in $x$ at an interior point $x_0$ shows that their span contains $(y-x_0)^k$ for every $0\le k\le p$. For $m-p+1\le i\le m$, the span $\xi_{i+p}-\xi_i$ is strictly positive and factoring gives $\psi_{i,p}-\psi_{i-1,p}=-(\xi_{i+p}-\xi_i)\psi_{i,p-1}$. Differentiate the degree-$p$ local identity in $x$ and use the degree-$(p-1)$ identity and this difference formula to obtain $\sum_{i=m-p}^{m}B'_{i,p,\xi}\psi_{i,p}=p\sum_{i=m-p+1}^{m}\frac{B_{i,p-1,\xi}}{\xi_{i+p}-\xi_i}(\psi_{i,p}-\psi_{i-1,p})$. Comparison in the dual basis yields $B'_{j,p,\xi}=p\left(\frac{B_{j,p-1,\xi}}{\xi_{j+p}-\xi_j}-\frac{B_{j+1,p-1,\xi}}{\xi_{j+p+1}-\xi_{j+1}}\right)$ on this interval. The boundary lower-degree terms vanish by support; any zero denominator corresponds to an identically zero lower-degree spline and its term is zero. For indices outside the active range both sides vanish by support. [A1, F1, step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra]
source_lines.46: 4.1 Taking $k=0$ in step 3.1 gives $\sum_{i=m-p}^{m}B_{i,p,\xi}(x)=1$. Step 3.1 also shows that these $p+1$ active functions span $\mathcal P_p$ on the interval. Because $\dim\mathcal P_p=p+1$, they are linearly independent there and are a local basis. [A1, step 3.1, algebra]
source_lines.48: 4.2 Induct on $p$. If the knot multiplicity $\mu\le p-1$, the lower-degree splines in the recurrence are continuous there by induction, so the recurrence makes $B_{j,p,\xi}$ continuous; the derivative formula then makes its derivative $C^{p-1-\mu}$, hence $B_{j,p,\xi}\in C^{p-\mu}$. If $\mu=p$, a B-spline whose support crosses the repeated knot has one nonzero piece on either side, namely $(x-\xi_j)^p/(\xi_{j+p}-\xi_j)^p$ and $(\xi_{j+p+1}-x)^p/(\xi_{j+p+1}-\xi_{j+1})^p$; both one-sided limits equal $1$, while any B-spline not crossing it has zero endpoint value there. If $\mu=p+1$, the required order is $C^{-1}$ and no matching is asserted. [A1, step 3.2, F1, algebra]
